content.title: About
content.content: Scallops are bivalve mollusks from the family Pectinidae. "Wild caught" indicates they are harvested from their natural marine environment rather than farmed. Freezing preserves their delicate flavor, firm texture, and nutritional profile, allowing long‑term storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scallops can “swim” by rapidly clapping their shells together to propel themselves.
Scallop meat is considered a gourmet delicacy and is featured in many fine‑dining menus.
Unlike many seafood items, scallops require only a brief sear—about 1–2 minutes per side—to be perfectly cooked.
Wild‑caught scallops often have a more pronounced briny taste compared with farm‑raised ones.
Scallops are rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as zinc and magnesium.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides roughly 20 g of complete protein, essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Scallops contain very little saturated fat, making them suitable for low‑fat dietary patterns.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and red blood cell formation; scallops supply a substantial portion of the daily requirement.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Zinc, magnesium, and selenium in scallops help immune health, metabolism, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of EPA and DHA contribute to cardiovascular and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Individuals with shellfish allergies may experience reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Potential toxin contamination
items.content: Wild seafood can accumulate toxins (e.g., domoic acid) if waters are polluted; purchase from reputable suppliers.

items.title: Quality loss from improper thawing
items.content: Repeated freezing and thawing can degrade texture and flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Scallops are best quickly seared in a hot pan with a little oil, seasoned with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lemon. They can be added to pasta, risotto, salads, or grilled. For cooking, thaw them in the refrigerator and pat dry with paper towels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen scallops at –18 °C or lower in an airtight package. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze. Discard any scallops that develop an off‑odor or discoloration.
